stem.text: Group 2 carbonates decompose on heating to form the corresponding metal oxide and carbon dioxide.
The mechanism for this decomposition involves the carbonate ion breaking down to form carbon dioxide and oxide ions.
Add two curly arrows to the carbonate ion in Figure 2.1 to suggest a mechanism for this decomposition.

stem.caption: Figure 2.1
stem.alt: A carbonate ion drawn with C double-bonded to an O at the top and single-bonded to two O– atoms at the lower left and lower right, then an arrow to O=C=O + O2–.

guidance: I LP drawn / any charges on diagram.
ARROW 1 from O– to C–O bond (arrow can start anywhere on O).
ARROW 2 from C–O bond to the other O– .

points.text: one curly arrow from a lone pair on one O– to the C–O bond (forming C=O), and one curly arrow from the other C–O bond to the other O– (which leaves as O2–); either O– may be used; BOTH arrows [1]

markScheme.note: The MS answer is the drawn curly-arrow mechanism (two alternatives); shown as ms.figure.

figure.alt: Two versions of the carbonate ion with curly arrows. In each, one arrow goes from an O– to the adjacent C–O bond and a second arrow goes from the other C–O bond onto the other O–.

explanation.text: Each curly arrow shows a pair of electrons moving. The first arrow starts on one O<sup>–</sup> and goes to the C–O bond next to it: that pair becomes the second bond of a new C=O. Carbon cannot have five bonds, so a second pair must leave: the other arrow starts in the C–O bond to the other O<sup>–</sup> and ends on that oxygen. That oxygen leaves with both electrons as O<sup>2–</sup>, and what remains is O=C=O. Either O<sup>–</sup> can be chosen for the first arrow, which is why the MS shows two versions.

reasoningChain: Arrow 1: from a lone pair on one O⁻ to its C–O bond, making a C=O double bond.
Arrow 2: from the other C–O single bond to that O⁻, which leaves as O²⁻.
Check that the product is O=C=O + O²⁻ as shown in Figure 2.1.

inferredMistakes.text: Drawing the arrows the wrong way, e.g. from a bond towards carbon, or starting arrow 1 on carbon instead of on oxygen.
Breaking the C=O double bond instead of a C–O single bond, which would not give O=C=O.

stem.text: The radii of some cations are shown in Table 2.1.
Use the data in Table 2.1 to predict the trend in thermal stability of the metal carbonates containing these cations.

guidance: NO ecf. Bullets are all u / c.
A bullet 2 charge density of M2+ decreases.
CON bullet 3 stronger ionic bond linked to larger ionic radii.

points.text: (stability increases) as (ionic) radii increases / size of M2+ increases / or Pb2+ largest radii ora
less polarisation / distortion of carbonate ion / anion / CO3(2)– or less weakening of CO bond / C-O / C=O

explanation.text: All three cations have the same 2+ charge, so their polarising power depends on size. A smaller cation has a higher charge density and distorts the electron cloud of the large carbonate anion more, weakening its C–O bonds so the carbonate breaks up into CO<sub>2</sub> and O<sup>2–</sup> more easily. Cu<sup>2+</sup> (0.073 nm) is smallest, so CuCO<sub>3</sub> is least stable; Pb<sup>2+</sup> (0.120 nm) is largest, so PbCO<sub>3</sub> is most stable.

The MS marks the three bullets together for 2 marks (the order, the radius trend and the polarisation of the carbonate ion), and each bullet must be fully correct. Saying a larger cation forms a stronger ionic bond contradicts bullet 3.

reasoningChain: Note all three ions have charge 2+, so compare radii only.
Order the radii: Pb²⁺ > Ca²⁺ > Cu²⁺, so stability PbCO₃ > CaCO₃ > CuCO₃.
Explain: a larger cation has lower charge density and polarises (distorts) the carbonate ion less.
Less polarisation means the C–O bonds are weakened less, so more heat is needed to decompose it.

inferredMistakes.text: Reversing the order by assuming smaller cations give more stable carbonates.
Explaining the trend in terms of ionic bond strength or lattice energy instead of polarisation of the carbonate anion.

stem.text: Suggest why the solubility of the Group 2 sulfates decreases down the group.

guidance: A M1 ΔHlatt and ΔHhyd become more endothermic / positive.

points.text: M1 ΔHlatt and ΔHhyd (both) become less exothermic / less negative [1]
M2 ΔHhyd changes more / changes faster / dominant factor / becomes less exothermic by a larger extent [1] ora
M3 ΔHsol becomes less exothermic / less negative or ΔHsol becomes more endothermic / more positive

explanation.text: Use the energy cycle ΔHsol = ΔHhyd(cation) + ΔHhyd(anion) – ΔHlatt. Down the group the M2+ ion gets larger, so both the lattice energy and the hydration enthalpy become less exothermic. The sulfate ion is large, so the lattice energy depends mainly on it and changes only a little as the cation grows. The hydration enthalpy of the cation depends directly on the cation's size and falls much faster. Hydration therefore releases less and less energy compared with the energy needed to break the lattice, so ΔHsol becomes less exothermic (more endothermic) and the sulfates become less soluble.

reasoningChain: State that both ΔHlatt and ΔHhyd become less exothermic as the cation gets bigger.
State that ΔHhyd changes more, because the large sulfate ion dominates the lattice energy.
Conclude that ΔHsol becomes less exothermic / more endothermic, so solubility decreases.

inferredMistakes.text: Saying ΔHsol 'decreases', which is ambiguous for a negative quantity and is ignored by the MS.
Saying the lattice energy changes more than the hydration enthalpy, which is the explanation for hydroxides becoming more soluble, not sulfates.
Writing 'H latt' or 'lattice H' without the Δ symbol, which the MS penalises once.

stem.text: Magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub>, is sparingly soluble in water at 298 K.
Write the expression for the solubility product, Ksp, of Mg(OH)2. State the units for Ksp.

explanation.text: Mg(OH)2(s) ⇌ Mg2+(aq) + 2OH–(aq). The solid is left out of the expression and the coefficient 2 becomes a power, so Ksp = [Mg2+][OH–]2. Units follow from three concentration terms multiplied together: (mol dm–3)3 = mol3 dm–9.

reasoningChain: Write the dissolving equilibrium: Mg(OH)₂(s) ⇌ Mg²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq).
Ksp = [Mg²⁺][OH⁻]², with no term for the solid.

inferredMistakes.text: Including [Mg(OH)₂] on the bottom of the expression, as for a Kc.

stem.text: A saturated solution of Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> has a pH of 10.35 at 298 K.
Calculate the concentration of hydroxide ions, OH<sup>–</sup>, in mol dm<sup>–3</sup>, in this solution.

explanation.text: pH gives [H+] directly: [H+] = 10–pH. In any aqueous solution at 298 K, Kw = [H+][OH–] = 1.00 × 10–14 mol2 dm–6, so [OH–] = Kw / [H+]. An equivalent route is pOH = 14 – 10.35 = 3.65 and [OH–] = 10–3.65 = 2.24 × 10–4 mol dm–3. This step has no outcome of its own in the Group 2 section, so it is mapped to the pH calculation for strong alkalis.

inferredMistakes.text: Calculating 10⁻¹⁰·³⁵ and giving it as [OH⁻], i.e. stopping at [H⁺].
Using 10⁻¹⁴ × [H⁺] instead of dividing, giving a very small value.

stem.text: Use your answers to 2(d)(i) and 2(d)(ii) to calculate the value of Ksp for Mg(OH)2.

explanation.text: Each Mg(OH)2 that dissolves gives one Mg2+ and two OH–, so [Mg2+] is half of [OH–]: 0.5 × 2.24 × 10–4 = 1.12 × 10–4 mol dm–3. Substituting into Ksp = [Mg2+][OH–]2 gives 1.12 × 10–4 × (2.24 × 10–4)2 = 5.62 × 10–12. An answer from the incorrect expression [Mg2+][OH–] gets no ecf.

reasoningChain: Use the 1 : 2 ratio: [Mg²⁺] = ½ × [OH⁻] = 1.12 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³.

inferredMistakes.text: Taking [Mg²⁺] equal to [OH⁻] instead of half of it, giving 1.12 × 10⁻¹¹.
